_comment: THE EXPECTATION-SOURCE REGISTRY. Every check in this kit declares two
things: the SUBJECT it asserts about, and the ARTIFACT its EXPECTATION is
read from. `tools/expectation_lint.py` fails when those are the same
artifact and no waiver explains why.
This file exists because the same defect was found eight times by six
LLM-persona adoption walks, each time wearing a different hat, and the
operating architecture's own promotion rule says a prose rule that keeps
failing gets promoted to a mechanical layer. The design question 'where
does this check's expectation come from?' is now an answer every check
expectation_from: "inline" means hand-written literals in the checking
code. Those are the specification, they do not move when the code moves,
and they are deliberately out of scope.
ADDING A CHECK? Add a row. The lint cross-checks the fixture family
against hook_fixtures.py, so an unregistered fixture is caught; for
everything else, an absent row is invisible - the residual, named in

checks.subject: kit.config:FORBIDDEN_SPAWN_TIER
checks.reason: THE ORIGINAL INSTANCE. The payload names the tier the rule forbids, and both come from kit.config, so fixture and rule move in lockstep - weaken the key and the fixture weakens with it, still green. Unavoidable for a config-driven rule: the fixture's job is 'the hook honours whatever the config says'. Covered STRUCTURALLY instead: kit.config is in JUDGE_PATHS, so any uncommitted change to it reds the `judges` gate; and the fixture additionally asserts the deny REASON renders the configured tier, which a placeholder value cannot satisfy.

checks.subject: kit.config:MODEL_EXEMPT_TYPES
checks.reason: Same shape as fixture:j, same structural cover (kit.config in JUDGE_PATHS). Weaker in practice than j was: fixture c's payload is hard-coded, so widening the exempt list moves the hook's answer out from under an independent expectation and IS caught.

checks.subject: kit.config:PROTECTED_PATH
checks.reason: The payload is built from the configured path when one is set. Narrowed twice since: when the path is UNSET the payload uses a synthetic probe no config can name (so an unconfigured tripwire can no longer pass by matching its own placeholder), and the accept-set is now exactly `ask` when no cert-green token exists rather than {ask, allow}. Structural cover: kit.config in JUDGE_PATHS.

checks.subject: kit.config:PROTECTED_PATH
checks.reason: As fixture:l, for the Edit branch.

checks.subject: .claude/settings.json
checks.reason: INSTANCE 6, and only half-closable. Whether the hook is wired can only be read from the settings file itself; there is no second source for the harness's intent. What WAS closable is startability - the script a matched command names is now checked against the FILESYSTEM, an independent artifact, and a missing one reports UNSTARTABLE. Residual, accepted: a settings file that is internally consistent and wrong (wired to the correct path of the wrong hook) reads as armed.

checks.subject: the escape-rate table in the judgment ledger
checks.reason: NOT a waiver - recorded because this gate's expectation is split and the split is the interesting part. The LINE FORMAT and the CEILING both live in verify.py's `escapes` entry, inside JUDGE_PATHS, so raising the ceiling is a reviewed commit; the DATA is the ledger table, which is deliberately NOT in JUDGE_PATHS because it is the subject being measured and putting it there would make every ordinary ledger append invalidate certification. The residual that buys: an uncommitted edit to the table moves the published number within a run. Compensating control, and it is weaker than a proof: the number is printed on every certification, so a changed number is in the log. Stated in KNOWN-ISSUES, 'The kit's own numbers'.

checks.subject: tools/statusline.py:escape-segment
checks.reason: NOT a waiver - recorded because it is a cross-file binding and a reader should be able to see which file is the authority. The status board renders an escape rate; the number, the ceiling the sparkline is scaled against and the state word all come from escape_rate.py, which the board imports and calls. A board that parsed the ledger itself would be a SECOND parser of one table - the two-authorities class this kit's tools spend their selftests hunting - and it would drift from the tool module 03's `escapes` gate runs, so the board and the gate would publish different numbers from the same file, both green. The statusline selftest's authority section therefore imports escape_rate.py and requires the rendered percentage, the ceiling and the state word to be the tool's, with a forced red that changes the tool's number and requires the board's to move with it. THE CEILING CLAUSE IS BOUND ON THE REPORT THE BOARD PRODUCED, not on one the test handed the ceiling to: spec-side review measured the difference by replacing the ceiling inside `escape_state` with a literal 40.0 and passing 90/90, because the check then in place only proved that `report()` echoes its own argument. That line is now labelled a PRECONDITION and the binding reads `escape_state(...)[1]['ceiling_pct']`, which is the value the board actually scales against; the same mutation now goes red naming that check. The class has precedent - KNOWN-ISSUES round 19 records a silently drifted gate ceiling as one of this kit's own escapes. Residual, stated: that section is the one part of that selftest which touches a filesystem, and when the tool is not reachable (the board copied out of a kit checkout) it reports UNAVAILABLE rather than passing in silence.

checks.subject: tools/statusline.py:tick-ramp
checks.reason: NOT a waiver - recorded because the expectation is deliberately NOT a literal. Whether a console can display the sparkline's block characters is a property of its code page, so the check asks the platform's own codec table (encode the ramp with the stream's encoding name and see whether it raises) rather than carrying a hand-written list of encodings that can. A literal list would be the same defect as a hard-coded `sys.platform == 'win32'` branch: wrong in both directions, since a Windows terminal set to UTF-8 draws the blocks and a POSIX host under LANG=C does not. The selftest drives the derivation with cp1252, cp437, ascii and an unknown encoding name and requires the ASCII ramp for each, so an edit that hard-coded the block ramp goes red. Residual, stated in the function's own docstring: an in-process check cannot see a console that misreports its code page, and the board's other segments draw block characters unconditionally, which predates this segment and is unchanged by it.

checks.subject: QUICKSTART.md
checks.reason: Not self-referential by artifact - the checkpoints are hand-transcribed from the document into the walker, so an edit to one does not move the other. That is also its weakness, and a different one: the walker can drift out of date with the prose it transcribes. It runs the COMMANDS, not the explanations. Named in KNOWN-ISSUES as a residual.

checks.subject: modules/03-verification/verify.py:git_excluded
checks.reason: The control for the SHIPPED exclusion probe, where check:judged-paths-not-excluded covers only how the startup assertion reacts to an injected answer. The phase plants a real ignore rule over a real judge path in a real repository, in both rule shapes, and compares the runner against `git check-ignore` run independently. It exists because the first version of the probe corrupted every path it asked about and all three gates stayed green: an injected-answer check cannot see a transport defect.

checks.subject: tools/kit_render.py:rendering
checks.reason: Not self-referential by artifact, and deliberately so. document_order() renders the same templates BY HAND - a person's transcription of QUICKSTART - and phase 13 requires the tool's rendering to match it byte for byte (CLAUDE.md, the collaboration profile, TOKEN-LEDGER.md) and key for key (the structural settings merge). The two authorities are kept apart on purpose: the walk must never call the tool and the tool must never read the walk, or the kit loses its only independent expectation of what a rendered file looks like. When they disagree the arbiter is neither of them - it is the QUICKSTART step the hand model transcribes, and on this phase's first run the document ruled for the tool. Scope: this row covers the RENDERING sub-steps only; the guard assertions in the same phase are registered separately at smoke:phase13-render-guards. Residuals: the walk can drift out of date with the prose it transcribes; and the walk copies three of the four ledgers unrendered at Step 7, so JUDGMENT-LEDGER, FAILURE-FLOOR and LESSONS are checked against Step 7's printed checkpoint rather than diffed - every slot they carry is already covered by the CLAUDE.md byte-diff, and TOKEN-LEDGER is hand-rendered because RATIO_CEILING appears nowhere else.

checks.subject: tools/kit_render.py:containment
checks.reason: The same phase also asserts the two containment guards END TO END - a real subprocess, a real target repository, a real kit checkout - and those expectations do not come from the hand model. Guard 1 is measured by pointing a run at the kit clone and checking the kit tree afterwards; guard 1b by a LEDGERS_DIR that climbs out of the target and checking that the outside directory was never created; guard 2 by hashing every hand-rendered file before and after. The tool's own selftest proves the same refusals in process, which cannot see a filesystem that disagrees with the decision layer - the same argument smoke:phase12 makes about the exclusion probe.

checks.subject: modules/03-verification/gate_line.py:pure-layer
checks.reason: NOT a waiver - recorded because it is a cross-file binding and a reader should be able to see which file is the authority. The adapter's expectation is not a literal somebody typed: it is what pytest actually reported when `--capture-golden` ran the six fixture suites in `examples/pytest_suites/`, committed as captured. The pure layer is then required to rebuild those lines and those verdicts exactly. Regenerating the golden file is a reviewed commit for the same reason - recapturing over a defect would install the defect as the new expectation. Residual, stated: the LIVE half (re-running pytest and comparing) needs pytest installed, and this kit's CI deliberately downloads nothing, so there the selftest prints LIVE HALF NOT RUN with the reason rather than passing in silence.

checks.subject: modules/04-ledgers/escape_rate.py:small-n-denominator-floor
checks.reason: NOT a waiver - an accepted residual, recorded where the check lives. The derived floor (ceil(100/ceiling)) makes the per-round ceiling gate partition-sensitive: the same evidence split into sub-floor rounds exits 0 where one round of it exits 1, and nothing mechanical fires on a sustained run of sub-floor rounds. The compensating disclosure is loud rather than gated - the cumulative rate and trend carry every escape, and the SMALL-N line prints on every such run naming the round, its item count and the floor - but its only reader is a person. Accepted by the owner's 2026-08-23 ruling over the alternatives on record (UNCOUNTABLE hides a real number; an unconditional red makes red mean nothing).

checks.subject: modules/04-ledgers/escape_rate.py:DEFAULT_CEILING
checks.reason: NOT a waiver - recorded because this check closes a measured two-authorities defect and a reader should be able to see which authority is which. The escape-rate ceiling is written twice as an operative value: the `--ceiling` literal in the runner's `escapes` gate command, and `DEFAULT_CEILING` in the tool. Nothing related them, and spec-side review measured the consequence - a copy of the tool with `DEFAULT_CEILING` at 90.0 published `ceiling 90.0%` from the standalone command the documents tell an adopter to type, while the same tool through the gate published 35.0, both green. `escape_rate.py --selftest` section F now reads the runner's source and requires agreement: the same cross-check shape as the fixture/registry and doctor/registry families, and it reads a genuinely different file from its subject. A THIRD spelling in `.github/workflows/kit-ci.yml` was deleted rather than bound - that step now passes no `--ceiling` and takes the tool's default - so two authorities remain and they are bound. Residual, stated: section F is the one part of that selftest that touches a filesystem, and when the runner is not reachable (this tool copied out of a kit checkout) it reports UNAVAILABLE rather than passing in silence.

checks.subject: tools/kit_doctor.py:KIT_VERSION
checks.reason: Two artifacts on purpose. The stamp records which kit release a tree was adopted from; the constant records which release the tools came from. Neither can be checked against the FILES - a version stamp is a claim by whoever last copied - but the two disagreeing is exactly the state a partial re-copy leaves behind, and that is mechanically checkable.

checks.subject: kit.config
checks.reason: The rule for 'is this key configured or still an example value' is imported from the shipped hook rather than re-implemented in the doctor. A fourth reader of that rule is the arrangement that produced the original defect.

checks.subject: modules/03-verification/verify.py:GATES
checks.reason: Three disjuncts, two of them structural properties of the gate table judged against hand-written rules (a require pattern with no capture group; a floor of 1 or less), and the third read from the FILESYSTEM (no docs/ORACLE-<gate>.md page). Registered as inline because the two rules that decide vacuity are hand-written literals; the filesystem half is named here so the row is not read as covering less than it does.

checks.subject: .claude/cert-green.json
checks.reason: Whether a token still covers the tree is git's answer (the newest commit touching CERT_PATHS is contained in the token's sha, and those paths are clean). What the check ALSO does is print the honest label on every run - the token is unsigned and forgeable by anything that can write a file - and that half has no expectation source because it is not a measurement. It is a disclosure, and it is the control.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's FAILURE-FLOOR.md
checks.reason: The anti-ratchet, promoted out of prose. The floor's own demotion-review section says every rule quiet for N stages gets RETIRE, DEMOTE or RE-AFFIRM at each phase gate, and nothing checked it - the owner's question was 'what is checking the lessons'. The window comes from the config key, NOT from the floor: a check that read its own threshold out of the file it judges could be cleared by editing that file, which is the class this registry exists for. The stage-to-day conversion is derived from the floor's own distinct firing dates because no file in an adopting repository relates stages to days, and the arithmetic is printed on every run so the threshold can be argued with. Residual, stated in the finding rather than here alone: rows reading `never` or `unknown - predates recording` cannot be dated and are reported as NOT MEASURED rather than counted either way, and the check reads a clock, so a project that has simply stopped recording looks stale - which is the correct reading for an anti-ratchet.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's rules file and newest checkpoint
checks.reason: The other half of the anti-ratchet, and the only ceiling in this kit derived from a measurement of the kit's own shipped documents. The rules file is re-read at the top of every session; the module-01 template states 'keep it SHORT' three times and nothing measured it. DIGEST_CEILING_LINES = 325 by the four-step method TOKEN-LEDGER.md gives for the cost ratio: (191 rendered template lines + the 90-line measured checkpoint norm) x 1.15, rounded up to the nearest 25, with the arithmetic printed on every run, green included. The FIRST OBSERVATION IS BOUND TO ITS SOURCE: --selftest measures modules/01-governance/CLAUDE.md.template live and requires it to still render to 191 lines, so if the template grows the derivation's input has moved and the selftest goes red naming both numbers - the same binding shape as check:escape-ceiling-agrees, built because that ceiling drifted silently once already. Residual, stated: n = 2 observations, one project, LOW confidence, and the check counts lines without judging whether any line earned its place.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's LEDGERS_DIR and collaboration profile
checks.reason: The file names Level 1 installs are the kit's shipped skeletons, and the doctor carries them as a literal because an adopted tree has no modules/ directory to read. The literal is held to the shipped set by a --selftest cross-check that runs whenever the tool sits in a kit checkout, so a renamed skeleton fails here rather than in an adopter's tree.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's Level-1 documents
checks.reason: The shipped-value half of this check reads the kit's shared rendered-text rule, imported rather than re-implemented - tools/adoption_smoke.py phase 9 asks the same question about the same class of file and now reads the same constant. The first version of this check carried a one-element list of its own and reported HEALTHY over six documents titled 'Example Project': two readers of one rule, drifting, which is the class this registry exists for. The clause the check implements - no surviving slot, no template header block, one shipped value allowed through by name (RATIO_CEILING) - is specified by the QUICKSTART Step 7 and Step 8 checkpoints. The marker words are literals in the tool, cross-checked against the shipped templates by --selftest, which also reads kit.config.example and requires every shipped example value that reaches a Level-1 document to be caught by the shared rule.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's kit.config
checks.reason: The shipped example is the registry of every key the templates interpolate, so it is the only honest expectation for 'does this config carry them all' - and it is a different artifact from the config being judged. Built because LEVEL-1.md step 2 prints `cp kit.config.example ./kit.config`, which on a repository that already has a config destroys every answer in it, and the reason an adopter reaches for that command is usually a key that renders as an unfilled slot. The check names the missing keys and names the destructive remedy as destructive in the same red. Residual: it judges PRESENCE of keys only - whether a value is an answer or a shipped example is doctor:l1-rendered's question, on the documents they render into. When no kit.config.example can be found the check reports UNKNOWN rather than passing.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's LEDGERS_DIR
checks.reason: The kit's four ledger filenames are fixed - the doctor hard-codes them and LEDGERS_DIR is the only thing an adopter can move - so on a repository that already keeps ledgers the install has three possible outcomes and the documents name none of them. Two of the three used to be green: install alongside, and overwrite. Measured on this kit's own program repository, which had LESSONS-LEARNED.md beside the kit's LESSONS.md and TOKEN_LEDGER.md beside TOKEN-LEDGER.md, every check green over two documents answering one question. The expectation is the shipped skeleton set, carried as the same literal doctor:l1-documents uses and held to modules/04-ledgers by the same --selftest cross-check. Comparison is on a normalised stem (case, punctuation and the .md suffix removed) with containment counted as collision, because the measured spellings differed only by a hyphen and a suffix.

checks.subject: kit.config:KNOWLEDGE_DIR
checks.reason: Whether the value is a configured answer or the shipped example is decided by the kit's shared placeholder rule, imported rather than re-implemented - a fourth reader of that rule is the arrangement that produced the original defect. The one departure is stated in the judge: for this key NONE is a decision (kit.config.example says to set it when there is no knowledge base outside the repo), so the NONE case is answered before the shared rule is consulted, and whether the named directory exists is the filesystem's answer.

checks.subject: the adopting repository's collaboration profile:INTERVIEW
checks.reason: The three states an interview status may hold are defined by the shipped profile template's STATUS block. --selftest reads that template and requires the shipped line to be judged UNANSWERED, so the pattern is proven against the artifact it was written for rather than against a copy the test wrote itself.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: The round-22 defect replanted: a quotation attributed to `DECISION-BRIEF.md` whose words are not in it. Inline literals - the control writes both the sentence and a source that does not contain it, so they are the specification rather than a reading of the tool's own output.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: Shape A, the parenthesised attribution, forced red on an invented quotation. Inline literals: the sentence and the source are both hand-written in the control.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:flatten
checks.reason: THE CONTROL THAT KEEPS THIS TOOL HONEST. The round-22 review reported a real quotation as fabricated because its grep was line-oriented and the source wrapped across a newline. The control asserts BOTH halves against inline literals: a line-oriented search misses it, and flatten()-based matching finds it. Without this the tool does not merely miss defects, it manufactures them.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: Found by the forced-red run rather than by design: the first build excluded newlines from the quoted string itself, so a quotation wrapping at the LINTING document's own margin was never seen and a planted fabrication read clean. Inline literals, including the blank-line bound that stops an unpaired quote mark swallowing whole paragraphs.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: Found by the first live run, which returned five findings of which three were this single class: a file reference in an earlier paragraph pulled onto an unrelated quotation. Inline literals, asserted for both attribution shapes.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: A reference in a previous markdown table cell must not attribute a quotation in this one - measured on KNOWN-ISSUES.md, where it was this tool's last remaining false positive before the rule landed. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: With two documents named before one quotation the nearest owns it, and the farther one must not also be made to answer for it. Inline literal; this is the precision half of the proximity heuristic.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:MIN_WORDS
checks.reason: The word floor separating a quotation from a named output line such as `0 skipped`. Asserted in both directions against inline literals: a short literal is not checked, a long one is.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: A document quoting itself is not an attribution. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:quote_is_in
checks.reason: The clean half - a quotation that IS in its source passes, with a locator and without one. A checker that has only ever been red is as untested as one that has only ever been green. Inline literals.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:WAIVERS
checks.reason: The waiver table is scoped to the case it names, covers nothing else, and every shipped waiver carries a non-empty reason - the same rule this registry applies to its own waivers. Read from WAIVERS itself, which IS the specification of what is waived.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:attributions
checks.reason: Found by a live run against the register row written to record this tool: an odd number of quote marks inside one markdown table cell made the pattern pair one phrase's CLOSING quote with the next phrase's OPENING quote, capturing 300 characters of prose as a quotation. A quotation does not cross a cell boundary either. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:REGISTER_DOCS
checks.reason: A findings register quotes text AS IT WAS when the finding was raised, beside a disposition that usually reads FIXED, so those words are absent from the current tree by construction. Exempted as a document class rather than one waiver per row, with the count printed on every run. Asserted in both directions - the register is exempt, an ordinary page is not - against REGISTER_DOCS itself, which IS the specification of which documents are exempt. Residual, disclosed in the tool and in the round entry: a genuine miscitation written into the register is exempt too.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:RECALL_FLOOR
checks.reason: Round 26's evaluation read (m4) found a real ten-word attribution the lint could not see, and section E passed anyway because it asserted only that SOME attributions were found. A presence count is not recall. RECALL_FLOOR names four attributions the shipped kit really contains - across two documents and both locator forms - and asserts each twice: extracted from its document, and its quotation present in the document it names. The expectation is the kit's prose rather than an inline literal on purpose, since a literal keeps passing while the pattern's reach shrinks underneath it, which is the failure this row exists to catch. Proven red-provable by reverting shape B's glue to its pre-round-27 form, which reds exactly the m4 row and no other.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:flatten_with_lines
checks.reason: WAIVED, and the lint was right to raise it - flagged on its first run, before any waiver was written. Subject and expectation are two functions in ONE file, so a single edit could move both and this check would stay green. It is kept in that shape deliberately, because the property being asserted IS an agreement between two normalisations and there is no third artifact that defines what the agreement should be. What makes it worth more than a tautology: the two are independently implemented - flatten() is a regex substitution, flatten_with_lines() is a character walk - so they agree only by both being correct, and the equality is asserted over EVERY SHIPPED DOCUMENT THE LINT ENUMERATES rather than over a literal the test wrote, so the input is outside the tool. The count is deliberately not restated here: it was 48 when this row was written at round 27 and 49 once round 28 shipped modules/08-collaboration/CAPSULE.md, and a number frozen in a reason field goes stale on the next document added while nothing checks it - the R28-3 finding in KNOWN-ISSUES.md. Residual, accepted and stated: an author who rewrites both functions in lockstep passes. Structural cover: tools/ is in JUDGE_PATHS, so an uncommitted change to either one reds the judges gate.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:quote_line_spans
checks.reason: The clean half of the window layer, against an inline literal whose line numbers the control writes itself: a quotation wrapping across two source lines reports the span it really occupies, a locator naming only its FIRST line still overlaps, and a range wider than the quotation contains it. Overlap rather than containment is what lets the tolerance be zero, so these three are the controls that keep the window check from manufacturing findings against correct citations.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:quote_in_window
checks.reason: THE FORCED-RED HALF, and the round-22 defect's actual shape: right words, wrong lines. Four assertions against inline literals - a locator one line past the quotation is a finding, one elsewhere in the file is a finding, the presence check alone still reports the words as present (which is precisely the gap this closes), and a tolerance of one line would pass the off-by-one case. That last assertion holds the shipped tolerance's justification as a test rather than as prose: the tightest of the six round-26 defects sits one line outside its cited range, so any tolerance above zero is blind to it.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:line_span
checks.reason: Which locators produce a window at all. A LINE form yields one, a single line yields a one-line window, a SECTION form such as ` Step 4` yields none so the attribution is checked for presence only, and an absent locator yields none. The last assertion checks the extractor carries the locator through to the caller, which is the join between the shipped pattern layer and the new window layer. Inline literals.

checks.subject: tools/citation_lint.py:quote_line_spans
checks.reason: A phrase may legitimately occur more than once in a document, and a locator naming EITHER occurrence is a correct citation. Without this the window check would invent findings against documents that repeat a phrase - the same manufacturing failure the wrapped-quote control prevents one layer down. Asserted in all three directions against an inline literal: both spans are reported, either one passes, and a locator naming neither is still a finding.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: ROUND 24's F1 REPLANTED: `ONBOARD.md` said Step 0 was nine lines while `QUICKSTART.md` Step 0 printed ten, a count that travels between documents and that nobody re-derives. Inline literals - the control writes both the claiming sentence and the ten-line section it names, so they are the specification rather than a reading of the tool's own output.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:table_rows
checks.reason: The local shape forced red: a stated count over the table it introduces, with a row missing. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: The checkpoint shape forced red: a count in the paragraph under the fenced block it counts. This is the site `QUICKSTART.md` corrected in round 23 while the cross-document copy in `ONBOARD.md` was left behind, so the control holds the half that was right as well as the half that was not. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: THE CONTROL THAT KEEPS THIS TOOL FROM BEING A DEFECT GENERATOR. A checker that has only ever been red over a stale count would turn every correct sentence in the kit into a finding; this asserts the same shape with the right number passes. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:countable_lines
checks.reason: Blank lines inside a fenced block are not countable lines. Inline literal; the countable-line definition is a judgment call and each of its clauses is asserted separately.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:countable_lines
checks.reason: A whole-line comment is not a command, and a TRAILING comment does not stop its line being one. Asserted in both directions against an inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:CONTINUES
checks.reason: FOUND BY THE FIRST LIVE RUN, NOT BY DESIGN, and the sibling of the citation lint's most important control. `QUICKSTART.md` Step 4's pwsh block is three commands on four physical lines, the third a pipeline continued on the next; the tool reported that correct sentence as a defect until a line ending in `\`, `|` or a backtick was counted with the line it continues onto. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:table_rows
checks.reason: The header row and the `|---|` separator are not data rows. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:list_items
checks.reason: A list with blank lines between its items is one list, and a continuation line is not an item - the shape most of this kit's numbered lists actually have. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:list_items
checks.reason: An indented sub-item belongs to the item above it and is not a top-level item. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: The false-positive floor, and the tool's largest declared blind spot: a count phrase with no locatable target is SKIPPED with the count printed, never guessed at and never failed. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: A colon inside a paragraph that keeps going introduces nothing. Inline literal; this is half of the narrowing the first live run forced, the other half being that the count phrase must OPEN the introducing paragraph.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:section_fence_count
checks.reason: A named section holding two fenced blocks is skipped rather than guessed at - a wrong target manufactures findings, which is worse than missing them. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: A document reference in a previous markdown table cell does not carry a count phrase in this one - the same rule the citation lint learned on this register's own rows. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:LINE_NOUNS
checks.reason: A cross-document count whose noun is not a line noun is skipped: no parser decides which lines of a block are selftests, or what counts as a document. Inline literal.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:REGISTER_DOCS
checks.reason: A findings register records what a count USED TO BE beside its correction, so checking those against the fixed tree asks the wrong question. Exempt as a document class with the count printed on every run, asserted in both directions against REGISTER_DOCS itself, which IS the specification of which documents are exempt. Residual, disclosed in the tool and in the round entry: a genuinely wrong count written into the register is exempt too.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:WAIVERS
checks.reason: Every shipped waiver carries a non-empty reason - the same rule this registry applies to its own waivers. The table ships empty in v1 and the assertion still holds, which is the point: it is the rule that binds the first waiver anyone adds. Read from WAIVERS itself, which IS the specification of what is waived.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:WIDE_COUNT
checks.reason: ROUND 24's REVIEW, m2: the tool CHECKS one..twenty and up to three digits, and phrases above that ceiling ('thirty lines', 'twenty-five commands', '1024 lines') were matched by nothing - not checked, not skipped, and absent from the skip total the docstring calls the disclosure. The review proved it by planting five false counts written with the word 'ninety' and watching all five vanish. The ceiling is deliberate and stays; what this control holds is that a phrase above it is now SKIPPED with a reason of its own. Inline literals - the control writes the phrase and the block it sits over, so both are the specification rather than a reading of the tool's own output.

checks.subject: tools/count_lint.py:claims
checks.reason: The other direction of count:vocabulary-ceiling, and the reason the disclosure pass is safe to add: a number INSIDE the checking vocabulary is still decided by the checking pass and is NOT also counted as a skip. The two patterns match disjoint number tokens; this control is what goes red if a later edit makes them overlap and inflates the skip total with phrases the tool actually checks. Inline literal.

checks.subject: checks-registry.json
checks.reason: The registry can only be checked against itself for internal consistency - there is no independent source for what a check's expectation ought to be. What it therefore cannot catch is an entry that is simply ABSENT. Narrowed for SIX families now, whose ids are recovered from the source and cross-checked both ways: the hook fixtures in hook_fixtures.py, the doctor's checks in tools/kit_doctor.py, the escape-rate tool's negative controls in modules/04-ledgers/escape_rate.py, the gate-line adapter's golden fixtures in modules/03-verification/gate_line.py, the citation lint's negative controls in tools/citation_lint.py, and the count lint's negative controls in tools/count_lint.py. The doctor was the reason to generalise the cross-check rather than trust the author - ten unregistered checks in one commit would have grown this blind spot faster than the lint that discloses it - and the escape-rate tool arrived with a set of them, every one reported by this cross-check on its first run before any were registered. Everything outside those six families still depends on the author adding a row. Stated as a residual in KNOWN-ISSUES rather than presented as closed.
